newsitem.title: UK: UK pension funds fear double tax hit under Labour.
newsitem.headline: UK pension funds fear double tax hit under Labour.

text.p: Britain's pension fund industry is facing a potential double blow as a result of tax changes if Tony Blair's Labour party wins Thursday's election.

Industry players said the planned imposition of a windfall tax on privatised utilities and possible changes to the Advance Corporation Tax (ACT) could play havoc with pension fund allocation and valuations.

The National Association of Pension Funds (NAPF) told Reuters that pension funds hold some 28 percent of shares in privatised British utilities, and would bear the brunt of the windfall tax Labour plans to implement.
The outlook for ACT is less clear.

Industry sources say Labour has not fully considered the consequences of such a move, and plan a major lobbying campaign in the coming months as the party looks to raise the revenue needed to fund its election pledges.
Labour could scrap the tax altogether or reduce it, and some players expect the changes to be part of a wider overhaul of taxation.
ACT, currently set at 20 percent, is levied from a company's gross profits at the same time as dividends are paid to shareholders.
It can be offset against a company's corporation tax liability, which means that it does not increase a company's overall tax burden.

Tax-exempt organisations such as pension funds benefit from a higher rate of ACT because they can claim more cash back from the government, so they would bear the financial brunt of any Labour government's plans to drop the rate.

There is a precedent for increasing revenue by lowering ACT. In 1993, Chancellor Norman Lamont lowered the ACT rate to 20 percent from 25 percent, a move which raised an extra billion sterling in government revenue.
In a recent survey 10 of 20 finance and managing directors of leading quoted companies said they expected a reduction in ACT.
Tim Congdon, Lombard Street Research director, said the abolition of ACT and the associated ACT tax credits would raise six billion sterling and would be easy to present in political terms.
He said that a halving of ACT would hurt post-tax profits and share valuations.

John Rogers, director of investment services at the NAPF, said an incoming Labour government could look to move early to alter ACT, and the association was lobbying hard to try to head off possible changes.
But Ian Carstairs, head of UK equities at fund manager Invesco, said he expected any ACT changes to be implemented late in Labour's term.

He said preference share market yields were implying a five percent lower ACT rate. If no tax changes were anticipated the differential over bond and gilt prices that would exist should be 150 to 170 basis points, and currently this was running about 50 basis points above that.
But any changes were likely to come in a package.
"They are talking about investment, over-distribution, not enough money being put back either to training or capital investment, (and) the decline of the manufacturing base."
He said Labour would be foolish to think that it could have a concrete view on changes to corporate tax before coming to power, and without the help of the civil service.
"Those things would be likely to be later rather than earlier," he said.
Carstairs said ACT changes would start the ball rolling and could see shifts in asset allocation.

"Because they will not be able to claim the tax back the effective returns they will be seen to be earning from this asset class...will be seen to go down. Therefore the actuarial assumptions will make that asset class apparently less attractive."
That may mean that pension funds have to consider the proportions they have in different types of assets.

"It may create apparent funding requirements which effectively becomes a call on the corporate sector. If it is a call on the corporate sector you have got to fund it, you have got to pay less tax. The whole thing is clearly a massively complicated problem."

The NAPF has said the removal of tax benefits would result in the need for an extra two billion sterling a year in contributions from companies. This would be tax-deductible and thus corporation tax revenue would be lower.
Rogers said that since the cut to 20 percent in ACT in 1993, two key issues have changed for pension funds.
He said fewer pension funds were in surplus, so there was less slack between pension fund income and the need to have the funding position improved.

Also, the minimum funding requirement has only come in since 1993, and now any shortfalls on funding have to be made up quickly, thus increasing company contributions and reducing the corporate tax take.
On the windfall tax, Rogers said industry members were patient long term investors, holding their shares since they were privatised.
